title: He Erased Every Object From His Paintings in the 1930s. At 73, on a Greek Cruise, He Started Drawing Them Again.
standfirst: In December 1933, working at a makeshift table in his first wife's Paris flat, Ben Nicholson carved the relief that pushed British painting toward its most complete break with the object. Three decades, two more marriages and a war later, a cruise round the Greek islands sent him back the other way.

sections.heading: A Table Built From a Table, in His Wife's Flat
sections.body: In December 1933 Nicholson was staying at the Paris flat of his first wife, the painter Winifred Roberts, its windows looking out over the Seine. He had no proper studio there, so he built one: the top of a second table set onto a smaller one, propped up with cross-pieces. On it he carved a board into two circles, one large and one small, with arcs scored outward from each into loose, unresolved rings. He left every false start visible rather than sanding it away — paint thinned in places, built up in others, so the object kept a record of its own making. He showed it the following year with [Unit One](https://www.theartstory.org/artist/nicholson-ben/), the group he had co-founded with Henry Moore, Barbara Hepworth and Paul Nash, under the plain title Two Circles. It is usually counted as his [first completed relief](https://www.piano-nobile.com/news/357-insight-no.-157-ben-nicholson-december-1933-first-completed-relief/).

sections.heading: By February He Had Stopped Using Colour at All
sections.body: Within three months Nicholson had gone further. In February 1934 he made a relief in white alone, its two circles and their surrounding arcs drawn with a ruler and a compass rather than judged by hand. Where the first relief kept the evidence of change, this one erased incident altogether — no tone, no visible brushwork, nothing to say a person had made it. It became the first of what are now called the White Reliefs, made between 1934 and 1937 and usually treated as Britain's clearest arrival of the abstraction that had already reorganised Paris. There was no object left to name in them. For a few years the ambition was a picture that answered no question about what it was of, only about how it was made.

sections.heading: His Father Painted Portraits. He Started by Copying Him.
sections.body: Nicholson's father, William Nicholson, was one of the most sought-after portrait and still-life painters in Edwardian London, and Ben's own earliest paintings were still lifes worked in his father's manner — a reputation he grew up inside rather than beside. It was Picasso's work, encountered in 1921, that gave him a way out: an engagement with Cubism that became his main occupation once he started making regular trips to Paris in the early 1930s. Between 1932 and 1934 those trips put him in the studios of Picasso, Braque, Brancusi and Arp, and eventually Mondrian's — visits that did more than any manifesto to move him from Cubist still life toward reliefs with no still life left in them at all.

sections.heading: "As If We Were One Person"
sections.body: By 1932 Nicholson had moved into 7 The Mall in Hampstead, the studio Barbara Hepworth had taken with her first husband, the sculptor John Skeaping, before their separation. Of the life he and Hepworth built there he wrote, that same year, that they could "live, think & work & move & stay still together as if we were one person." Naum Gabo, Laszlo Moholy-Nagy, Piet Mondrian, Henry Moore and Paul Nash all worked within a few streets, several of them refugees from fascism on the continent, and their neighbour Herbert Read called the group "a nest of gentle artists." In 1937 Nicholson, Gabo and the architect Leslie Martin edited the results into [Circle: International Survey of Constructive Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle:_International_Survey_of_Constructivist_Art), a single hefty volume of essays and photographs laid out by Hepworth. It was meant to be the first of a series. It was also the last — no second issue ever appeared.

sections.heading: Three Marriages, Three Working Artists
sections.body: Nicholson married three times, and each time to a woman with her own practice to protect. Winifred Roberts, his first wife, was a painter whose career ran alongside his for eighteen years before they separated in 1938. Barbara Hepworth, his second, was already an established sculptor when their relationship began; they married that same year and had triplets, and it was with her that Nicholson moved to Cornwall in 1939, helping turn the fishing town of St Ives into what became Britain's other centre of modern art for the next two decades. That marriage ended in divorce in 1951. His third wife, Felicitas Vogler, was a German photographer; they married in 1957, and it is from the years travelling Europe with her afterwards, mostly based in Switzerland, that his last body of unfamiliar subject matter comes.

sections.heading: Thirty-Four Years On, He Drew a Chapel Again
sections.body: In 1967, at seventy-three, Nicholson spent part of a holiday cruising the Greek islands and the Turkish coast, filling sketchbooks with chapels, columns, sundials and harbour clutter. Over the following year those drawings were worked up into a suite of etchings, [Greek and Turkish Forms](https://www.porthminstergallery.co.uk/exhibitions/88-ben-nicholson-greek-turkish-forms/), reduced back into line rather than left as travel sketches — Aegean among them. It is a strange place to end up for a man who had spent 1934 trying to remove the object from art altogether: thirty-four years after the white relief that erased incident on purpose, he was naming what he saw again. The suite has never ranked among his major work, its [auction prices modest](https://www.myartbroker.com/artist-ben-nicholson/series-greek-turkish-forms) next to the reliefs — but the record it leaves behind is of a Cubist's eye returning, in old age, to pick one specific stretch of coastline out of the world, exactly the habit he had spent thirty years training out of himself.
